A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MEAL, with matching core benchmark, methods, and experiments. All 18 pages of v1 and 27 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original continual-learning baseline results, architectural ablations, difficulty comparisons, and repeated-task plasticity experiments in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and adds results concerning agent count, observability, rewards, curriculum learning, and designated roles in Section 5 and the appendices.

M1.justification: V2 extends the benchmark with direction-aware observation masking, individual rewards, and chef/waiter roles that restrict permitted interactions and can switch across tasks (Sections 5.6–5.7; Appendices D and H). These substantively change observations, capabilities, and reward assignment. The core layout generator and existing actor–critic framework largely persist.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate all three Overcooked difficulty levels; higher difficulties already appear in v1 Appendix C.1. V2 adds evaluated scenarios with one and three agents, partial observability, heterogeneous roles, and individual or sparse rewards. These extend sensing conditions, agent capabilities, and task requirements.

E2.justification: AGEM joins the five existing CL comparators in v2 Table 2. Higher-difficulty comparisons expand from v1's EWC analysis to the full six-method set. V2 also evaluates MAPPO against IPPO in Figure 8 and introduces independently trained IPPO as the explicit forward-transfer reference.

E3.justification: V1 states that task identity is hidden at evaluation and evaluates previously seen tasks; v2 specifies known evaluation identities and evaluation on all sequence tasks. V2 replaces the primary plasticity metric with baseline-relative forward transfer, averages forgetting over final windows, and removes the replay prohibition. Appendix E adds an equal-budget curriculum comparison. Appendix B.1 narrows the stated MLP depth from {2,3} to two layers. These reported revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The original five-component ablation and repeated-task plasticity study remain. V2 adds tests of agent-count effects, reward design, partial observability, designated roles, and curriculum ordering. Appendix I and Figure 13 add qualitative failure cases involving single-pot fixation, deadlock, and role collapse.

E5.justification: Five seeds and the existing Level 1 average-score and forgetting intervals are retained. V2 explicitly identifies the appendix table intervals as 95% confidence intervals. However, Figure 7 drops v1 Figure 6's explicit ±1 standard-error specification for plasticity bars, leaving their convention less clear under the general confidence-interval statement. No increase in runs is documented.

E6.justification: V2 replaces primary plasticity-score entries with forward-transfer results and adds extensive comparator and scenario results. The newly tabulated Level 3 comparison ranks Online EWC at 0.306 above EWC at 0.178 in average score. Existing Level 1 average-score and forgetting entries remain identical. Separately, plasticity FPR changes from 1.228 to 0.906 for three repetitions and from 0.896 to 0.866 for ten repetitions (v1 Table 3; v2 Table 4), with its definition retained.

T1.justification: Section 4.5 revises mathematical evaluation definitions: endpoint forgetting becomes window-averaged forgetting, and mean current-task performance is replaced by normalized AUC-based forward transfer. Section 3 also relaxes the restriction on retaining past data. The soup-bound derivation, generator/validator complexity arguments, and appendix plasticity definitions remain substantially unchanged; no new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central MEAL/JAX novelty claim remains, but v2 broadens the claimed benchmark contribution to controlled observability and agent count. Its conclusion adds claims about curriculum benefits, reward design, and centralized-critic interference. It drops the handcrafted-layout contribution and v1's assertion that parameter-isolation methods fail to scale.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantial mechanism explanations involving cumulative versus decayed Fisher penalties, centralized-critic interference, team-size non-stationarity, role bottlenecks, and multi-head protection against plasticity loss. It removes the fully observable/two-agent applicability restriction while retaining domain and continual-setting limitations. Some concluding interpretations are stronger than the evidence: individual rewards have positive aggregate forward transfer in Table 5 despite the conclusion's negative-transfer claim.

D1.justification: The detailed implementation appendices largely persist. V2 adds optimizer and activation settings, AGEM memory/projection sizes, task-boundary handling, observation-window dimensions, and role-assignment instructions. Listing 1 now returns soup counts rather than counts multiplied by 20; this does not establish a rescaling of reported scores. Hardware, seed identifiers, and the code-access link remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 retains the earlier references and adds ten works supporting AGEM, curriculum learning, partially observable benchmarks, and reward/cooperation discussions. The dedicated related-work discussion and the central positioning as a CMARL benchmark with end-to-end JAX acceleration remain largely intact.

P1.justification: Much of the original exposition is retained. V2 consolidates baseline and forgetting discussions, moves normalization into Section 4.5, and relocates the old appendix difficulty/plasticity analyses into Appendices F and G. Local explanations and the conclusion are rewritten, and authorship and acknowledgments change.

P2.justification: The layout examples and generator illustrations are redrawn and reordered. V2 combines existing and new panels in Figure 3, expands per-task plots in Figure 16, restructures Table 2 across difficulties, and places full uncertainty tables in Appendix J. New trade-off plots, observability illustrations, failure examples, and experimental tables substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens the benchmark's diagnostic value. V1's evidence centered on homogeneous, fully observable two-agent learning; v2 directly tests coordination through agent-count, visibility, reward, and role controls, including roles that prevent solo task completion. Broader comparators and explicit single-task references better distinguish retention from transfer. These address important gaps in support for the CMARL benchmark claim. Less explicit plasticity uncertainty reporting and overstatement of individual-reward negative transfer remain weaknesses, but do not outweigh these substantive gains.
